# Who gets asked

## No one asks the **[Data Scientist]{.accent}**… {.center}

::: {.notes}
No one asks the person who actually has to write the code.

Legitimacy beat, gently: "I've been that Data Scientist. I spent the last
few years moving a team from dplyr to Polars, and that migration is
where everything in this talk comes from."
:::

## Thesis: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*A language migration should optimize for the easiest option for the person who has to write the code.*
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM, SLOWLY)
The hot take: the API matters more than speed, cost, or support.

This is the one decision that determines how much friction the team absorbs.
:::

## This is not a Polars talk {.center}

::: {.fragment}
We use a migration from my experience — **dplyr → Polars** — as the worked example to demostrate our thinking.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You can swap in your own, the concepts carry across any code migration.
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
"I want to be clear about what this talk is and isn't. It is not a Polars talk."

[click] 
"I'm going to use one migration I've lived through — dplyr to
Polars — to show you what 'easiest' looks like in practice."

[click] 
"If your migration is SQL to Spark, or SAS to R, swap it in.
The argument is about the choices you make, not the tool."

This is the slide the focus group was missing. Don't skip it.
:::

## By "API" I mean the function signature {auto-animate="true"}

Not a web API. The shape of the contract: what you pass in, what you
get back, what you have to learn to use it.

::: {.api-example}
**The `sum` API**

```r
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Quick fence around the word before going on: API here is the literal
function signature — the arguments and the return — not REST.

"This is the sum API." Don't explain it. Next.
:::

## By "API" I mean the function signature {auto-animate="true"}

Not a web API. The shape of the contract: what you pass in, what you
get back, what you have to learn to use it.

::: {.api-example}
**The `filter` API**

```python
df.filter(pl.col("paid"))
```
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is the filter API." Same idea, different language. Move.
:::

# What "easiest" actually means

## Easiest means: productive on day one {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Early]{.accent} wins

- The [thin-slice]{.accent} effect
:::

::: {.notes}
Verbal signpost: "So what does easiest mean? Two things. First: can the
Data Scientist be productive immediately?"

[click] Early wins — real code that runs on day one, before anyone has
mastered environments, classes, or types. Impresses superiors; feels
good.

[click] Thin-slice — first impressions aren't accurate, but they have
more predictive power and persistence than we'd like. We're judgemental
animals. Callback: my first ten minutes installing Python was a thin
slice, and it stuck.

Not fair, but real, and it has to be managed.
:::

## Day one

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
**dplyr**

```r
df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  select(
    is_customer = str_like(persona, 'cust'), 
    revenue = sum(c_across(rev1:rev8), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
**Polars**

```python
df.filter(pl.col("status") == "paid").select(
    is_customer = pl.col('persona').str.contains('cust'), 
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(cs.starts_with('rev'))
    )
```
:::

::::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = it works in ten minutes.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Don't explain the code — the room should recognize it instantly.

The pipe became a dot. filter is filter, select is select. That is the
entire lesson for day one.

Say it as a property of the CHOICE, not of Polars: "This is what the
easy option looks like on day one — it works in ten minutes. Whatever
you're migrating to, this is the test."
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*Day one decides whether people keep going.*
:::

::: {.notes}
Not all APIs are created equal — some are thin wrappers exposing every
private method. A user-friendly framework pays off while people are
still coming up to speed on everything else.

The goal is comfort, not full control of a complex system.
:::

## Easiest means: the same shape of thought {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Easy [syntax]{.accent} is a virtue
- Import your [philosophy]{.accent}
:::

::: {.notes}
Verbal signpost: "That's day one. The second thing easiest means is
about every day after: the Data Scientist doesn't have to relearn how to
think about data."

[click] Easy syntax — other options leaned on verbose, heavily-typed
languages that added friction before anyone got to the actual work.

[click] Import your philosophy — Polars' expression API preserves the
dplyr way of thinking about data, not just its syntax. select,
transform, filter, aggregate — no detour through OOP, strong typing, or
imperative loops.
:::

## Same thought, different language

`sum(revenue[status == "paid"])` becomes:

```python
pl.col("revenue")
  .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
  .sum()
```

::: {.fragment}
**Easiest = the same sentence, in a new language.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is transfer, not onboarding: once you know the syntax, does the
system let you keep thinking about data the way you already do?

Subset a vector by a condition, then reduce it. Same thought. The R
version is a bracket; the Polars version is a chain — but it's the same
sentence.

[click] Nobody wrote a for loop. The vectorized mental model came with
us. That's the property to look for: the option where your old
sentences still parse. Not "Polars is great" — "this is what easy
looks like."
:::

## Same thought, every column

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**dplyr**

```r
df |>
  mutate(across(
    starts_with("rev"),
    \(x) x * 1.1
  ))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Polars**

```python
import polars.selectors as cs

df.with_columns(
  cs.starts_with("rev") * 1.1
)
```
:::

::::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = you didn't learn a new way to think.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Column selectors: the same idea in both — pick columns by a rule, apply
one expression to all of them.

[click] Same idea, both sides. The chain is the pipe; the expression is
the thing inside `across`. Again — the point isn't that Polars has
selectors; it's that the easy option is the one where the Data Scientist
didn't have to learn a new way to think.

Morale beat lives here: when everyone writes it this way, code is
readable and reviewable across the team. Shared idioms mean the whole
team has the *same* migration, not eight different ones.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Some days, you don't need to learn anything new.
:::

::: {.notes}
Migrating is already information overload — it doesn't all have to land
on day one. You don't take Calc 4 before Calc 1.

Once people are comfortable, they move on to the fancier stuff on their
own, and make better-informed decisions about it.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Productivity
:::

::: {.fragment .big-word}
→ Familiarity
:::

::: {.fragment .big-word}
→ Confidence
:::

::: {.aside}
We wrote this migration up in a long-form piece with the Polars team.
:::

::: {.notes}
Verbal signpost: "Put the two pillars together."

[click] Productivity — day one works.
[click] Familiarity — the shape of thought carries over.
[click] Confidence — and confidence is the thing a migration actually
runs on. Morale isn't a separate goal; it's what you get when the first
two are true.

Footnote, one sentence: we liked it enough that we wrote it up publicly
with the Polars team. Don't linger.

Cycle 2 of 3: "That's what it means to pick the easiest option for the
person who writes the code."
:::

# Ask the Data Scientist

## Next time you're in that room {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Ask: *does it work on [day one]{.accent}?*
- Ask: *does my old [sentence]{.accent} still parse?*
- Ask: *who [asked]{.accent} the Data Scientist?*
:::

::: {.notes}
Verbal signpost: "So here's what I'd like you to take out of this room."

You will be in a migration meeting. Finance, leadership, tech, and
cyber will all have an opinion. Three questions to bring:

[click] Day one — can someone write real, useful code before they've
mastered environments and types?

[click] Old sentence — take a line you write every week in the old
language. Does it translate, or does it need a detour?

[click] Who asked the Data Scientist — if the answer is "no one," you're
the one who has to.

This is the call to action. Land it, then the last picture.
:::
